this is the f*cking walkthrough I wish someone had sent me before my first AI agent.

most people don't fail at the model.
they fail at everything around it.

so here's the end-to-end path, no fluff:

> JOB - one responsibility in one sentence. not "help me with stuff". "own my inbox overnight."
> CONTEXT - the docs, inbox or repo it's allowed to read. nothing else.
> TOOLS - start read-only. sending, paying and merging come later.
> DECIDE - the small yes/no calls go to a cheap decision layer like Jev. the big model only writes.
> GUARD - a hook that checks every risky step before it runs.
> PROOF - a log of what it decided and why, so you can read it in the morning.
> SHIP - run it on one real task tonight. not a demo.

if you lose two weeks in the underbrush, it's almost always because you skipped JOB and GUARD.

give it responsibilities, not tasks.
let it run.
read the log.
fix one thing.
run it again.

that's how your first agent ends up in production by tomorrow instead of next month.

OpenAI's dots doesn't answer your question.

it shows you where the answer would have to come from.

and that should scare every tool that ships pretty paragraphs.

here's how the map works:

> SPREAD - your question gets broken into the individual claims an answer would need
> ANCHOR - each claim gets pinned to the exact span in your own documents that carries it
> VOID - claims with nothing behind them stay empty. no filler, no guessing
> LINK - claims that depend on each other get connected
> READ - you get the finished map back as points. never as a paragraph

a normal answer hides its own gaps.
the sentences are smooth, and the part with nothing underneath reads exactly like the rest.

dots refuses that trade. an unsupported claim shows up as an empty point. impossible to skim past.

the LINK step is the sharp part.
one hollow anchor lights up every claim sitting on top of it at once.

so you don't get "something feels off".
you get "this document is missing".

fluency has been doing the convincing in every AI tool so far.
here it has nothing to hide behind.

if you run agents on your own data, steal the rule: no span, no claim.

save this before you trust the next smooth answer.

Opus 5.5 is 2x the price of Sonnet 5.5 on paper.

in a long agent loop it's closer to 1.26x.

and the reason is the cost nobody prices in: switching models mid-session.

hand a Sonnet 5.5 session to Opus 5.5 at 300K tokens of context and you pay $1.50 before Opus has read a single file or written a single line.

that's not work.
that's just rebuilding the cache for the new model.

so the classic trick, "cheap model first, smart model when it gets hard", quietly charges you every time you switch.

what I'd do instead:

> pick the model per job, not per mood
> if the loop is going to be long, start it on the model that will finish it
> keep the start of your prompt stable so the cache keeps hitting
> let a cheap decision layer like Jev make the small routing calls instead of swapping models

paper price is per token.
real price is per finished task.

full breakdown is in Gipp's guide. bookmark it before your next long run.

how it works
the idea is to run christmas accounts that post every day, with everything made by ai and an agent running the whole thing. you can start with one account, or run a few at once in different niches.
everything starts from the data. the agent pulls the christmas content that already works, and that tells you what to post, what it should look like and what to sell.
the whole system runs on a few tools.
the agent is the part that runs the full pipeline, like hermes, grok bot, a dot in chatgpt or whatever you use. an agent can take actions on its own, so it can research what's trending, write the posts, schedule them etc.,
a scraper pulls public posts from tiktok, instagram and facebook so the agent can study them. i use apify, and the agent calls it with an api key, which is basically a password that lets your agent use the service on your account.
for the video model, seedance 2.5 right now makes the best looking videos, and gemini omni is the cheaper option for everyday clips.
and a posting tool schedules everything to tiktok and instagram or facebook.
and if you want to run paid ads too, whop ads lets you run them on facebook and instagram straight from your whop account.
each account can get paid three ways from the same audience. merch through printful, a digital product on whop, and gift guides with affiliate links. for ex, one person watching your videos might buy a mug, a christmas planner and a gift from a guide, all in the same season.
start with the data
the same kinds of christmas content do well every single year, so the first thing the agent does is pull it.
it uses apify to grab the most viewed and most saved christmas posts on tiktok, instagram and facebook from last november and december, which shows you what peaks every year. then it pulls the top christmas posts from the last couple of weeks, which shows you what's already starting to pick up this year.
pull christmas content broadly before you pick a niche, like cooking, baking, decorating, gifts, kids' crafts, hosting and so on, and let the numbers show you where the views and the saves actually are.
for each post the agent notes the hook, which is the first line or first second that makes someone stop scrolling, the format, the length, the topic, and what it asks the viewer to do at the end. for videos it reads the transcript, and for slideshows it reads the text on every slide. it also notes whether the post shows a face, and what the setting and style look like.
the most useful part is the comments. people ask stuff like where something is from, how to make something, or what to get their dad, and those questions are basically a list of things people want to buy.
"it looks something like this:"
the rule is to copy the format. so if decorating a tree in one take is doing well, your version has your own tree, in your own setting, even when you remake it shot for shot.
making the content
with the skill file done, the agent can start making posts. most accounts end up as a mix of short videos and slideshows, and one post a day is enough as long as it goes out every single day.
there are three ways to make a video. text to video, where you just describe the shot. image to video, where the image model makes the first frame using the look from the skill file and the video model brings it to life, which is best when the setting or the persona has to match. and remaking a video that's already working.
